spatialkit

spatialkit draws analysis regions, which it calls cells, from where your observations are, instead of borrowing boundaries drawn for other purposes, and summarises point data onto them with a count, a standard error and a pooled value for every cell. It then scores regression models on cross-validation folds that hold out whole blocks of space, and marks where a fitted map extrapolates.

The problem this solves

You have observations at points and need values over areas. The usual move is to borrow boundaries that already exist: ZIP code areas, census tracts, counties, sales territories. They were drawn for mail delivery, enumeration or politics, so part of any answer aggregated onto them comes from the partition. This is the modifiable areal unit problem: the same observations, aggregated under different boundaries, can give different conclusions.

spatialkit draws the cells from the data, in three steps:

  1. Pick a cell count. resolution_profile() and select_resolution() set it from a size of 4.5 observations per cell by default, and report the leave-one-out error of the cell values. Given a ladder of counts, the profile scores each one against the spatial structure of the observations.
  2. Place the cells. get_voronoi_seeds() places seeds by density-weighted k-means, so cells are small where observations are dense, and build_tessellation() grows Voronoi cells from them (or lays hex or square cells, or Delaunay triangles), clipped to your study area. build_tessellation() numbers the cells from their geometry, so the same seeds in a different row order give the same cell IDs.
  3. Summarise. summarize_by_cell() gives each cell a count, a mean with its standard error, and a pooled value: the cell’s mean pulled toward the mean of the observations in the 8 nearest cells (nearest by the centroid of their observations). When the cell means stand in for a population mean, it can correct the standard errors for autocorrelation within the cells, which on a correlated field can double them or more.

The first figure shows a simulated field on 280 random sites in North Carolina, aggregated onto three kinds of cells, about 30 of each: Voronoi cells from density-weighted seeds, a hex grid and a square grid.

 

The next figure cuts the same field at three cell counts, each cell showing its pooled value. resolution_profile() scores each count by the leave-one-out error of the pooled values at that count. The error is 0.33 at 12 cells, 0.18 at 62 cells (the count the default size of 4.5 observations per cell gives) and 0.18 at 140 cells (two per cell). The 12 cells blur the hotspot in the east. At 140 cells the error is within one standard error of the default’s. vignette("resolution") covers how the count is chosen.

 

The second half of the package tests the result. Three model backends (random forest, GWR and a Bayesian GP) sit behind one spatial_fit class, so they can be scored on the same folds. Cross-validation holds out whole blocks, of a grid by default, which can be sized from the data’s own autocorrelation range or matched to the locations a map will predict at. An area-of-applicability estimate marks where the resulting score applies. All of it is built on sf, and each function that measures a distance moves a lon/lat layer into a projected CRS first.

Random folds put a test point’s neighbours in the training set, so a model that can memorise location is scored on points it has nearly seen. Block folds hold out whole blocks instead; the quick start below shows the difference in RMSE.

 

Scope

  • Regression, with one exception. fit_rf_model() and fit_gwr_model() fit a numeric response and refuse a logical, factor or character one; fit_gwr_model() also refuses an integer-coded two-valued response and points to GWmodel::ggwr.basic(). The exception is fit_bayesian_spatial_model(), which also fits a binary response under brms::bernoulli(), and a factor or character response under brms::categorical() or an ordinal family. cv_bayes() refuses the categorical and ordinal families, because it scores one predicted number per row.
  • Vector data only. There is no raster input or output: predict_surface() returns an sf POINT layer, which you convert yourself if you need a SpatRaster. The models work on points: prep_model_data() and coerce_to_points() reduce lines and polygons to points.
  • No areal or lattice models. Moran’s I here tests residuals for spatial structure. There is no CAR, SAR or spatial-lag fitter.
  • No spatio-temporal folds. Every fold scheme is spatial; none holds out time.

Installation 

install.packages("spatialkit")

The development version installs from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit")

sf, dplyr, logger, digest and FNN install with it. Optional packages switch on the model backends, variograms and plots; Get started lists which does what. If you are upgrading from 2.0.0, the changelog lists the defaults that change results and the argument that restores each.

Quick start

A simulated field of 400 observations in a 1,000 m square, with one weak measured predictor w:

library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(42)
n  <- 400
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$w <- rnorm(n)
# Mostly a smooth spatial field (exponential, effective range 3 x 80 = 240 m),
# with the weak predictor on top.
xy$z <- 0.5 * xy$w +
  as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 80) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n)) +
  rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
site <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)

Set the cell count, draw Voronoi cells from the data and summarise onto them:

size <- select_resolution(resolution_profile(site, "z"))
size
#> Resolution by size: 89 cells
#>   size        : 4.5 rows per cell, the default (obs_per_cell); 400 rows / 89 cells = 4.49
#>   cells       : density-weighted k-means++ starts (power 1, 8 neighbours)
#>   estimate    : pooled toward the 8 nearest cells
#>   at this size: 0.0% of the rows are alone in their cell; median own weight 0.78
#>   loo         : 0.912 (one cell for the layer: 1.5)
#>   note        : the count is set by obs_per_cell = 4.5, the default; no
#>                 criterion chose it.

seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(n = size, sample_points = site)
tess  <- build_tessellation(seeds,
                            boundary = clip_target_for(site, quiet = TRUE),
                            method = "voronoi", quiet = TRUE)
asg   <- assign_features_to_polygons(site, tess$cells,
                                     polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
cells <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = tess$cells)

head(st_drop_geometry(cells)[, c("cell_id", "n", "resp_mean_z", "..se_resp_z",
                                 "..pooled_resp_z")], 4)
#>   cell_id n resp_mean_z ..se_resp_z ..pooled_resp_z
#> 1       1 4   1.3680408   0.3289247       1.0626423
#> 2       2 3  -0.2762594   0.1258383      -0.1086915
#> 3       3 3  -0.9436130   0.5218985      -0.6630103
#> 4       4 5  -1.9008715   0.1581262      -1.4425290

The default size gives 89 cells, each holding between 2 and 10 observations. Each row has a count, the cell mean, its standard error and the pooled value ..pooled_resp_z, the cell’s mean pulled toward its neighbours by a weight that grows with the cell’s count (?summarize_by_cell, “Pooled values”). That standard error is the one for the cell’s own mean when its points are spread through the cell. When the cell means stand in for the population mean, deff = "kish" widens each standard error for the correlation inside the cell; on these cells it multiplies them by 2.2 (median). ?summarize_by_cell says which to use when.

Then score a model. A random forest given the coordinates (include_coords = TRUE) can fit the training surface by memorising location. Score it on random folds and on blocks of at least 250 m, just above the field’s effective range (this needs ranger):

fr <- make_folds(site, k = 5, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
fb <- make_folds(site, k = 5, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 250,
                 seed = 1)

random  <- cv_rf(site, "z", "w", folds = fr, include_coords = TRUE)
blocked <- cv_rf(site, "z", "w", folds = fb, include_coords = TRUE)

c(random = random$overall$RMSE, blocked = blocked$overall$RMSE)
#>    random   blocked 
#> 0.9790119 1.1227029

On the same 400 observations and the same model, random folds give an RMSE of 0.98 and the blocks, built 332 m wide, give 1.12. The data and the model are the same; the random figure is the error of predicting among the samples, and the blocked one the error of predicting into gaps a block wide. A map’s error depends on where it predicts, and fold_separation() compares the folds’ distances from the training data with the map’s. On real data the range is estimated, by estimate_sac_range() or make_folds(auto_range = TRUE); vignette("spatial-cross-validation") covers that choice.

The pipeline

Steps 1 to 10 link to their section of the reference index, and every step to the article that shows it. ?spatialkit lists the same steps inside R.

Step Main functions Article
1. Prepare the data ensure_projected(), coerce_to_points(), prep_model_data() Get started
2. Measure spatial autocorrelation estimate_sac_range() Spatial cross-validation
3. Choose a resolution resolution_profile(), select_resolution() Choosing a resolution
4. Build the cells get_voronoi_seeds(), build_tessellation() Building cells and summarising them
5. Assign and summarise assign_features_to_polygons(), summarize_by_cell() Building cells and summarising them
6. Make folds make_folds(), fold_separation() Spatial cross-validation
7. Fit a model fit_rf_model(), fit_gwr_model(), fit_bayesian_spatial_model() Fitting and checking models
8. Cross-validate and compare cv_rf(), cv_gwr(), cv_bayes(), compare_models_cv() Spatial cross-validation
9. Choose predictors select_features_forward() Fitting and checking models
10. Predict a surface and check where it applies predict_surface(), area_of_applicability() Fitting and checking models
11. Report ensure_stable_poly_id(), sf::st_write() Exporting and reporting results

Citation 

citation("spatialkit")

This prints the package entry and the papers behind the methods spatialkit implements. Cite the paper as well as the package if you rely on area_of_applicability() (Meyer and Pebesma 2021), make_folds(method = "nndm") (Milà et al. 2022) or make_folds(method = "knndm") (Linnenbrink et al. 2024). Do the same for the model backends you use: the Hilbert space approximation in fit_bayesian_spatial_model() (Riutort-Mayol et al. 2023), permutation importance in fit_rf_model() (Strobl et al. 2007), coordinates as predictors and blocked validation in fit_rf_model() and cv_rf() (Meyer et al. 2019), and GWR, whose kernels and diagnostics follow GWmodel (Lu et al. 2014).
